content.title: Interesting idea but more experiments needed
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.review:
In this work, the authors propose an information theoretic objective for co-training, wherein two learners are trained together to predict the same label, z, from two "views", x and y, of the data. Unlike the classical co-training framework, the focus here is on the fully unsupervised setting. Also, here there is an asymmetry between the two views: it is easy to predict z from y, and the goal is to learn to closely match this prediction given only x. This is enforced using an information theoretic loss function.

I liked the formulation of the problem and the loss function itself. I can imagine that this is an idea that will find use in various scenarios. However, as of now, this is just a nugget of an idea that needs to be developed much more. The only experiment given in the paper gives somewhat underwhelming results. (Of course, this may not be the fault of the main idea itself, and may have to do with the other details in the experiment.) But to meet the bar for ICLR, I feel that the authors should present more convincing evidence. Also, in the process, they may discover crucial details that are important to get the idea to work well.

The authors themselves note that the experiments are preliminary and that "with just a little more experimentation" they hope to get stronger results. I share their optimism, and would encourage them to carry out these experiments and make a stronger submission.

Pros:
Promising/interesting idea

Cons:
Not fully developed
Thin experimental section

display_title: Interesting method and the formulation is precisely given. Experimental results are not strong.

content.title: Interesting method and the formulation is precisely given. Experimental results are not strong.
content.review:
This paper presents a novel algorithm for unsupervised learning based on information theoretic co-training. The objective is to find parameters that maximize the mutual information between x and y through hidden variable z without computing the probabilities of x and y directly. This means that this technique allows to find a structure from data in an unsupervised way without modeling x and y explicitly. The proposed method is applied to unsupervised learning of phonemes on TIMIT corpus. The experimental results show that the learnt representations correspond to the labeled phonemes 35.1% on all frames.

The idea looks original and the formulation is presented precisely. Comprehensive comparisons to related models are given. The experimental results are not very strong, but the authors claim that they are initial experiments and can be improved with just a little more experimentation.

The experiments could be improved to show the effectiveness of the proposed approach better. The experimental results show that it can learn something but it is difficult to know how good the number is. Probably, it is useful to compare the method with some simple baseline even if it is not the objective of the paper to achieve high accuracy. Also, I am not sure if the phoneme discovery is the best task for the experiments. If the purpose is to discover phoneme as accurate as possible, probably, one might take another approach. Probably, it is better to emphasize that this is just to show the ability of the approach. It will be useful to show a list of possible applications. If more experiments can be added with such applications, it will be great.

I would recommend to have a figure to explain the procedure of the algorithm, i.e., how to update phi and psi.

display_title: Interesting idea, but I would prefer to see more theoretical analyses

content.title: Interesting idea, but I would prefer to see more theoretical analyses
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.review:
The primary idea here is to find a discrete latent varable z that attempts to have large mutual information with both available (past) and unavailable (future) measurement instances, x and y respectively. The discrete nature of z makes estimating associeated entropy and conditional entropy expressions relatively easier (in contrast to work from late 90's and early 00's by Fisher, Principe, and others who explored the idea of using various information theoretic approaches in similar settings with NNs and other models). The idea is a variation of the information bottleneck concept where z has more freedom, therefore when attempting to find the best z that attempts to simultaneously maximize MI with x and y, it is important to penalize one (e.g. epply an upper bound or bledn into the objective with opposite sign/rate as in Eqn4) while favoring the other. The paper proposes to drop the second term in Eqn4 (in that case the MI of z and y is penalized (or could also be constrained from above). This paper presents then an approximation of the first objective which brings a tradeoff due to the approximation of H(z) with a model that has parameters \Theta. 

While we could ask the authors to do more experiments to improve our confidence in how this approach would perform in practice, this reviewer is in favor of a more theoretical guarantee, in the form of theoretical guarantees in certain situations. At the end of the day, we have a tradeoff to make in the information bottleneck scenario - we want to find z that has high MI with both past and future data; there is an associated Pareto front in which we can choose any point unless one of the objectives is constrained from above (in given specs). This paper assumes a particular model that makes z discrete, therefore its mutual information with x & y are immediately bounded by the discrete marginal entropy of z that is possible under any circumstance. The invoked structure on z already deviated us to the suboptimal region above the Pareto front; how much did we lose there (due to the model restriction on z)? Further, objective (3) assumes a particular linear combination of two objectives (which would imply together another Pareto front worse than the ones in (4) would imply, considering MI between z and x,y respectively would induce). How much did we lose by going to these bounds (i.e. how tight are these bounds in certain situations)?

While the importance of more numerical results to gain improved confidence in a given optimality objective for certain situations is not disputed, it is also very important to understand how the proposed approach behaves under some landmark theoretical conditions, so we can make continuity arguments about models and objectives, thereby get some ability to extrapolate theoretical conclusions to nearby practical operating conditions that we might encounter.

So in summary, it is quite important to understand what this objective does versus what information bottleneck or classical co-training objectives do in certain landmark circumstances with well specified theoretical characterizations.
